idiom_name: interface with one method per product kind + constructor funcs / driver registry
implementation_notes: Go has no abstract base classes, so the factory is a plain interface whose methods return other interfaces (Button, Slider), implemented by small structs - one per family - that name the concrete types. Family selection is idiomatic through a map of constructor functions or a registration function modelled on sql.Register, where a driver registers itself in init() and sql.Open looks it up by name; the database/sql split between the user-facing DB and the driver interfaces is the stdlib proof that this shape works at scale. Go 1.18 generics help only for single-product constructors (New[T]); a family contract stays an interface. For testability, define the factory interface in the same package as the client so tests can pass a mock without importing the production package.
pitfalls: Returning an interface containing a typed nil (*darkButton)(nil) produces a non-nil interface value; callers later dereference it and panic, so return a nil interface only for an explicit absence or a valid product on success.
Registration-style maps panic on duplicate names (sql.Register does so by design) and concurrent writes race; register during init or guard mutations with sync.RWMutex, then keep lookup read-only.
A factory interface with too many methods is un-Go-like: Go favors small interfaces composed from the consumer side, so split wide families into role-specific interfaces.
Requiring clients to switch on the family name defeats the interface; resolve the name at the composition root and inject the selected factory.
A map-based registry is read-mostly after initialization; do not mutate it concurrently with lookups unless the registry provides synchronization.
